Title: Echocardiography does not predict mortality in hemodynamically stable elderly patients with acute pulmonary embolism.

Journal/Date: Thrombosis research (2016)

MeSH Keywords: Aged, Aged, 80 and over, Cohort Studies, Echocardiography, Female, Humans, Male, Prospective Studies


--- ABSTRACT ---
[BACKGROUND]: The evidence on the prognostic value of transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) in elderly, hemodynamically stable patients with Pulmonary Embolism (PE) is limited.
[OBJECTIVES]: To evaluate the prevalence of common echocardiographic signs of right ventricular (RV) dysfunction and their prognostic impact in hemodynamically stable patients aged ≥65years with acute PE in a prospective multicenter cohort.
[METHODS]: TTE was performed by cardiologists. We defined RV dysfunction as a RV/left ventricular ratio >0.9 or RV hypokinesis (primary definition) or the presence of ≥1 or ≥2 of 6 predefined echocardiographic signs (secondary definitions). Outcomes were overall mortality and mortality/non-fatal recurrent venous thromboembolism (VTE) at 30days, adjusting for the Pulmonary Embolism Severity Index risk score and highly sensitive troponin T values.
[RESULTS]: Of 400 patients, 36% had RV dysfunction based on our primary definition, and 81% (≥1 sign) and 53% (≥2 signs) based on our secondary definitions, respectively. Using our primary definition, there was no association between RV dysfunction and mortality (adjusted HR 0.90, 95% CI 0.31-2.58) and mortality/non-fatal VTE (adjusted HR 1.09, 95% CI 0.40-2.98). Similarly, there was no statistically significant association between the presence of ≥1 or ≥2 echocardiographic signs (secondary definitions) and clinical outcomes.
[CONCLUSION]: The prevalence of echocardiographic RV dysfunction varied widely depending upon the definition used. There was no association between RV dysfunction and clinical outcomes. Thus, TTE may not be suitable as a stand-alone risk assessment tool in elderly patients with acute PE.
[CLINICAL TRIAL REGISTRATION]: http://clinicaltrials.gov. Identifier: NCT00973596.

[AIMS]: This study was designed to assess whether any difference exists among clinical, laboratory, electrocardiography and echocardiography parameters between older and younger patients diagnosed with APE.
[METHODS]: The study sample included a total of 635 patients with confirmed APE who were divided into two groups of older (65 years and older) and younger (younger than 65 years) individuals. key_findings.finding: In the most directly applicable study—prospective multicenter cohort of 400 hemodynamically stable adults aged ≥65 years with acute PE (PMID 27498122)—TTE did not predict 30-day mortality: RV dysfunction (RV/LV ratio >0.9 or RV hypokinesis) was present in 36%, but was not associated with mortality after adjustment (HR 0.90, 95% CI 0.31–2.58); it also did not predict the composite of mortality/nonfatal recurrent VTE (adjusted HR 1.09, 95% CI 0.40–2.98). Results were similarly null when ≥1 or ≥2 of six echo signs were used. The authors concluded TTE should not be used as a stand-alone risk tool in elderly stable PE. Limitations available from the abstract include reliance on varying, non-uniform RVD definitions and lack of full-text detail.

source_tools.relevance: Direct elderly stable PE cohort with adjusted mortality estimates and conclusion

key_findings.finding: A 2021 observational study of 635 acute PE patients, including 295 older adults (≥65 years), reported 30 in-hospital deaths overall: 21/295 (7.1%) in older versus 9/340 (2.6%) in younger patients. In multivariable logistic regression, basal RV end-diastolic diameter and TAPSE <16 mm were independently associated with in-hospital mortality, along with age, WBC, and LVEF. The abstract does not provide odds ratios, confidence intervals, or confirm that all participants were hemodynamically stable, so this is supportive but less directly applicable evidence.

source_tools.relevance: Older-adult subgroup, echo parameters, and in-hospital mortality outcome

key_findings.finding: In a retrospective cohort of 129 hemodynamically stable PE patients with median age 70 years (PMID 24461144), RV dilation, septal motion abnormality, RV hypokinesis, tricuspid regurgitation, and systolic pulmonary artery pressure (sPAP) >30 mmHg were evaluated as RVD criteria. Adding elevated sPAP improved discrimination for identifying RVD (AUC 0.796 for the combined definition vs 0.790 without sPAP; sPAP alone AUC 0.635), but the abstract reports no mortality analysis; therefore it cannot establish mortality prediction.

source_tools.relevance: Stable older cohort and detailed RV/pulmonary-pressure parameters, but no mortality endpoint reported

key_findings.finding: In 411 initially normotensive, hemodynamically stable acute PE patients (mean age 64±18; PMID 24412192), TAPSE was the strongest echocardiographic prognostic marker for a composite of 30-day PE death or rescue thrombolysis: adjusted HR 0.64 (95% CI 0.54–0.70), AUC 0.91. TAPSE ≤15 mm had HR 27.9 (95% CI 6.2–124.6), while TAPSE >20 mm had a 100% NPV for the composite; RV/LV ratio was weaker (AUC 0.638). Because the cohort was not restricted to elderly adults and the endpoint combined mortality with rescue treatment, this is indirect evidence rather than elderly-specific mortality evidence.

source_tools.relevance: Strong TAPSE predictive-performance data in stable PE, but not elderly-specific and composite endpoint

key_findings.finding: A large registry study of 4,478 hemodynamically stable PE patients (PMID 39442929; mean/age-stratified elderly-specific results not provided in the abstract) found lower TAPSE/PASP coupling predicted 30-day all-cause mortality. Adjusted OR was 1.32 (95% CI 1.14–1.52) per 0.1 decrease; thresholds were associated with mortality in low-risk (<0.40: aOR 5.88), intermediate-low-risk (<0.43: aOR 2.96), and intermediate-high-risk (<0.34: aOR 4.37) groups. TAPSE/PASP <0.44 improved net reclassification versus RV/LV >1 and ESC risk strata. Applicability to elderly patients is uncertain because elderly-specific estimates are not reported.

source_tools.relevance: Large stable-PE mortality study with TAPSE/PASP effect estimates; elderly-specific applicability uncertain

key_findings.finding: Other stable-PE cohorts show conflicting overall prognostic results: a prospective study of 214 stable outpatients found 1-month mortality 7/214, with RV dysfunction positive in 4 deaths versus negative in 3 (OR 2.0, 95% CI 0.4–9.3; P=.41; PPV 5%, NPV 98%), concluding TTE was not useful for prognostic stratification (PMID 17919415). A multicenter prospective cohort of 201 normotensive patients found no prognostic marker predicted PE-related in-hospital death/clinical deterioration; clinical score, troponin, and hypoxemia—not echocardiography—predicted all-cause mortality (PMID 19302447). Conversely, an external validation cohort of 869 stable patients with both echo and troponin found combined RVD plus elevated troponin associated with in-hospital death/clinical deterioration (8.8%; HR 14.2, 95% CI 1.94–104.16), while echo alone had low discrimination (C-statistic 0.59).

source_tools.relevance: Directly supports conflicting evidence and limited value of echo alone
Stable prospective cohort showing no echo-marker prediction of PE-related events
Stable cohort comparing echo alone with combined RVD+troponin model

key_findings.finding: Right-heart thrombus evidence is not elderly-specific or restricted to hemodynamically stable patients: the ICOPER analysis (PMID 12821255) included 2,454 PE patients, with baseline echo in 1,113; right-heart thrombi were associated with higher 14-day mortality (21% vs 11%) and 3-month mortality (29% vs 16%). This supports prognostic importance of a right-heart thrombus, but it should not be extrapolated specifically to stable elderly PE without subgroup data.

source_tools.relevance: Right-heart thrombus mortality estimates, with explicit limitation on elderly/stable applicability
